What repeat airborne laser scans reveal

Four headline takeaways comparing leaf-off USGS 3DEP LiDAR against 40 years of Landsat satellite imagery across Alabama, Tennessee, and Kentucky.

−79%

Standard winter satellite trends miss understory change

Removing the calibration jump between older and newer Landsat satellites cuts the 40-year winter trend from +0.033 to +0.007 per decade. Against repeat laser scans, neither winter (r = -0.00) nor spring (r = -0.05) NDVI tracks midstory change.

-29.1%

Repeated burning clears nearly a third of midstory crowding

Across topographically matched hardwood stands, plots burned three or more times hold nearly a third less 2–10 m woody crowding than unburned controls (up to -48.1% in southern Bankhead NF; pooled site-fixed-effects slope −0.064, p < 0.001).

-0.076 NRD

Repeat laser flights confirm fire works in Bankhead

In northern Bankhead NF (2012 to 2021), two or more burns lowered 2–10 m midstory change by -0.076 relative to unburned controls (d = -0.95, burn-unit p = 0.0001), unchanged after density-thinning sensitivity tests.

4–7 m

Surface fire works best below the midstory crossover zone

In 1 m cross-sectional height profiles, three or more burns outperform mechanical thinning plus fire at 1–4 m (p ≤ 0.01) while leaving first-return canopy above 10 m intact; mechanical thinning plus fire is stronger at 8–10 m (p ≤ 0.024) and opens the upper canopy (-0.067, p = 0.001).

Compare calibrated trends across Tennessee parks and forests

Evaluated strictly on the upland plateau surface (430 m elevation and above) using the repaired 10,282-hectare Fall Creek Falls boundary. Click any row to fly the map there.

Across the southern Tennessee plateau top as a whole, forest cover stepped down from 5,617 km² in 1985 to 5,135 km² in 2001 and has remained steady since (5,185 km² in 2024, +0.97% net since 2001 despite 1,129 km² of rotational timber harvest that grew back).
